claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1–4 and 6, run a paired representational study on open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Draw harmful intents from the public AdvBench and JailbreakBench datasets and apply public jailbreak templates from JailbreakHub; retain only intent–jailbreak pairs for which the unmodified intent is refused and the jailbreak is judged compliant by both a public HarmBench classifier and blinded human annotation. Add benign, topic-matched prompts as controls. Under deterministic decoding, record every head’s attention pattern, output vector, output norm, and contribution to refusal-versus-compliance logits over the prompt and first generated tokens. Compare each successful jailbreak with its unmodified harmful prompt to identify heads whose safety-associated activity is selectively reduced, while testing whether harmfulness remains decodable elsewhere using representations or harmful/refusal logit directions fixed before examining the test split. Correct for multiple comparisons and test whether the identified set is substantially smaller than the full head population and replicates across held-out intents, attack families, and models. Persistence of harmful-content information in non-suppressed heads, despite reduced activity in a small safety-linked subset, would support bypass rather than elimination; loss of such information throughout the network would support elimination, while broad changes across many heads would reject the selective-suppression claim. This experiment could be unnecessary if existing work provides public per-head activations for paired successful and unsuccessful jailbreaks, preregistered localization criteria, and held-out replication across attacks and models.

To address subclaim 5 and the causal part of subclaim 3, intervene on the candidate head subset localized in Experiment 1 without reselecting it. On held-out harmful prompts that normally elicit refusal, suppress candidate-head outputs by zero ablation, mean ablation, or graded scaling during the prompt and early response positions; measure refusal-to-compliance conversion using refusal rate, attack success rate, harmful-completion probability, and blinded human judgments. Perform the reciprocal rescue experiment by patching the corresponding head outputs from the unjailbroken refusing run into the successful-jailbreak run. Include equal-size random-head controls, norm- and layer-matched controls, complement ablations, sham patching, and benign prompts evaluated for helpfulness and fluency. A large, dose-dependent increase in harmful compliance from candidate-head suppression, together with restored refusal after reciprocal patching and little effect from controls, would show that suppressing this small subset is sufficient and that jailbreaks bypass an intact safety signal; failure of suppression to induce compliance would refute sufficiency, while only large distributed ablations working would favor a distributed mechanism. Existing public intervention traces showing both suppression and reciprocal rescue on held-out models and attacks could obviate this experiment.

To address subclaims 7–9, construct a genuinely zero-training harmful-input detector from the persistent representations identified in Experiment 1 and evaluate it on untouched public test sets such as JailbreakBench, MaliciousInstruct, Anthropic HH/red-team prompts, and benign Alpaca or MT-Bench prompts. Freeze the model, selected heads, token aggregation rule, and readout before evaluation; use no labeled examples or parameter fitting—for example, score each input by projecting the aggregated persistent-head residual contribution through the model’s existing unembedding onto a preregistered set of refusal-versus-answer token logits, and report threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC plus TPR at fixed FPR. If an operating threshold is needed, set it using an unlabeled or separately declared calibration set and report this distinction. Compare on identical examples with public dedicated safety models such as Llama Guard, WildGuard, and the HarmBench classifier, including clean harmful prompts, successful jailbreaks, paraphrases, multilingual examples where available, and benign hard negatives. Competitiveness should be defined in advance, such as AUROC within a stated margin and comparable TPR at 1% and 5% FPR, with bootstrap confidence intervals and cross-model replication. Competitive performance without fitted parameters would support direct, training-free readout; strong performance only after fitting a probe would reject the no-additional-training subclaim, and poor performance specifically on successful jailbreaks would undermine the persistence claim’s practical consequence. This experiment could be unnecessary if a public benchmark already reports frozen, parameter-free activation readouts and matched results against these dedicated detectors on held-out jailbreak and benign datasets.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 forms successful jailbreak/unmodified pairs and measures per-head activity and refusal-related contributions throughout the prompt and early response, while also testing whether harmfulness remains decodable in non-suppressed components. reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level localization and classification procedure that quantifies safety-related contributions and makes the resulting small head subsets reliable across analytic choices and held-out data.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct evidence that non-candidate components retain harmful-content signal during successful attacks, together with a perturbation test showing whether that signal is carried by those components.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution that separates contributions from the original harmful request and the attack template, allowing persistence to be distinguished from merely different sensitivity to harmful content.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set does not perform the required source-token versus attack-template attribution, so it cannot establish that the candidate head types behave similarly on the harmful request while diverging specifically on the attack template.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment distinguishes the bypass mechanism from a sensitivity confound by attributing each head's activation to the original harmful-request tokens and to attack-template tokens separately.

Proposed experiment 0 compares aggregate and per-head activity and decodability, while proposed experiment 1 supplies causal ablations, but neither decomposes a head's activation by those two token sources.
Therefore a difference observed under a jailbreak could still be explained by differential sensitivity to the combined prompt rather than selective bypass by the attack template.
The team would fail to learn whether the head types are indistinguishable on harmful-request tokens and diverge only on attack-template tokens: missing.

sufficiency_reasoning: As a set, the proposed experiments would test the central behavioral and representational claim: paired successful jailbreaks, residual harmful information outside a localized subset, causal suppression and rescue, and a frozen readout benchmarked against dedicated detectors. The remaining gaps are mechanistic rather than a wholesale absence of evidence: the proposed set does not explicitly perform token-level attribution to rule out generic harmful-content sensitivity, and it does not unambiguously measure the causal contribution of the non-target heads to the persistent attacked-state signal. Those ambiguities prevent the strongest version of the mechanistic claim from being fully settled.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired, layer- and component-wide measurement of safety-related activation on successful attacks versus the same requests without attack, capable of distinguishing global erasure from residual signal.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 constructs successful/unattacked pairs, records head-level safety-linked activity and refusal/compliance contributions, and explicitly tests whether harmfulness remains represented elsewhere versus being lost throughout the network. Its fixed directions and held-out replication provide a valid alternative to the reference's activation scan.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A filtered paired corpus in which the same harmful request is refused without the attack and succeeds with the attack, with enough variation in prompts and attack conditions to support within-pair inference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 retains exactly the needed refusal/compliance pairs using public harmful prompts and jailbreaks, with human and classifier checks, benign controls, held-out intents, attack-family replication, and multiple models.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A validated procedure for localizing and quantifying a small set of heads whose safety-linked contributions change under attack, with safeguards against arbitrary selection thresholds and statistical artifacts.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed study records every head's relevant activity and contribution, applies multiple-comparison correction, tests that the localized set is substantially smaller than the head population, and requires replication on held-out intents, attack families, and models. This supplies the discriminating localization and small-subset evidence without requiring the reference's particular scoring statistic or cutoff sweep.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal, dose-responsive intervention on the localized heads, evaluated on held-out harmful prompts with matched random and other nuisance controls and direct refusal-to-compliance outcomes.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 suppresses the prelocalized subset without reselecting it, varies intervention strength, measures refusal/compliance and harmful completion, and includes equal-size random, norm/layer-matched, complement, sham, and benign controls. Reciprocal rescue further strengthens the causal interpretation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal test that the non-target heads are a source of the persistent safety-relevant signal during successful attacks, by suppressing them under the attacked condition and measuring the resulting change in that signal.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 measures whether harmfulness remains decodable in non-suppressed representations, and Experiment 1 includes complement ablations. However, the proposal does not clearly require applying those complement interventions to successful attacked inputs while measuring the persistent internal signal itself; its stated outcomes focus mainly on compliance, refusal, and fluency. Thus it bears on the question but leaves the causal source of the persistent mid-layer signal ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment establishes persistence of the internal signal by suppressing the non-target head group on successful attack inputs and measuring the signal's change.

[2] Proposed experiment 0 can show that harmful information remains decodable outside the candidate subset, while proposed experiment 1 mentions complement ablations and mainly evaluates behavioral conversion.
[3] Persistence or behavioral effects alone do not establish that the non-target heads causally generate the persistent signal under the attacked condition.
[4] A team running the proposed set would therefore not cleanly learn the causal source and magnitude of the persistent signal that reference experiment 4 would have established.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution that separates information contributed by the original harmful request from information contributed by the attack template, allowing generic harmful-content sensitivity to be distinguished from the proposed mechanistic specialization.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments record attention patterns and compare paired activations, but do not attribute head activity to request tokens versus attack-template tokens or compare the two head groups on those token classes. No other proposed experiment supplies that rival-mechanism discrimination.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment distinguishes bypass specialization from the alternative explanation that the head groups merely differ in sensitivity to harmful content.
[2] The proposed set tests head suppression, persistence, and detector performance, but contains no token-level decomposition separating harmful-request tokens from attack-template tokens.
[3] Those experiments can show that a subset affects behavior and that harmful information persists elsewhere without showing why the two head groups differ.
[4] A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the observed head split reflects the claimed attack-template bypass mechanism rather than generic harmful-content sensitivity.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An out-of-sample, cross-model and cross-domain evaluation of a frozen, training-free harmful-input readout against the model's own safety behavior and dedicated safety baselines using comparable classification metrics.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 freezes the model, heads, aggregation, and readout before evaluation, forbids labeled fitting, evaluates multiple untouched harmful/jailbreak and benign datasets, compares identical examples with dedicated safety models, preregisters competitiveness criteria, reports AUROC/AUPRC and fixed-FPR performance, and includes cross-model replication. The proposed scope is different from the reference's exact benchmark and model counts but has comparable evidential force for the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence on successful jailbreaks that the heads outside the selectively targeted subset retain a measurable harmful-content representation, rather than the apparent persistence being confined to the targeted heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 explicitly tests harmfulness decodability in non-suppressed representations while comparing successful jailbreaks with their unmodified counterparts. A decoder is a different readout from mean absolute activation and directly establishes the claimed persistence of harmful-content information; causal suppression of that other group is not required by the claim that it continues representing the content.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution that separates the contribution of the original harmful request from the jailbreak-template tokens, allowing the selective-suppression account to be distinguished from a simpler difference in head sensitivity to harmful content.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0's paired comparisons, attention patterns, and per-head logit contributions bear on the localization question, but it does not explicitly decompose each head's activation by harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens. Thus it could show that a subset changes during successful attacks without resolving whether the apparent head-type difference is attack-template-specific or merely content sensitivity.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment uses token-level attribution to distinguish selective attack effects from the rival explanation that head types simply respond differently to harmful content.
Proposed experiment 0 compares whole prompt conditions and records attention-related quantities, but does not state a token-class attribution or an original-request-versus-template comparison.
Whole-prompt head differences can therefore be caused by added template tokens, changed context, or inherent sensitivity rather than selective suppression by the attack mechanism.

The proposed set would learn that localization and persistence occur, but would fail to learn whether the two head behaviors separate specifically on attack-template tokens rather than on the harmful request itself.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: As written, the proposed set would directly test the central claim: persistence versus elimination, selective localization, causal refusal-to-compliance conversion, persistence in other heads, and training-free detector performance against dedicated safety models. The remaining gap is mechanistic rather than a missing central endpoint: the set does not resolve the token-source confound that the reference attribution experiment was designed to rule out. Consequently, the team could decide the main behavioral and representational claim, but could not make the stronger attack-template-specific mechanistic interpretation without an explicit token-level attribution experiment.
